blocks.heading: Key Concepts
blocks.html:
• Heart pumps blood to meet body metabolic demands
  • Left side: pumps oxygenated blood to body (systemic)
  • Right side: pumps deoxygenated blood to lungs (pulmonary)
  • Frank-Starling law: increased stretch = increased contraction force (to a point)
  • Compensatory mechanisms: SNS, RAAS, ADH, BNP
  • Ejection fraction (EF): % of blood ejected per beat (normal 55-70%)

blocks.heading: Normal Values
blocks.html:
• EF normal: 55-70%
  • CO normal: 4-8 L/min
  • PCWP normal: 6-12 mmHg
  • BNP normal: <100 pg/mL

blocks.heading: What the Nurse Must Know
blocks.html:
• HFrEF (systolic): EF <40% — pump problem. HFpEF (diastolic): EF >50% — filling problem
  • Left-sided HF backs up into LUNGS (pulmonary edema)
  • Right-sided HF backs up into BODY (JVD, peripheral edema, hepatomegaly)
  • BNP rises with ventricular stretch — useful for diagnosis and monitoring

blocks.heading: NORMAL FUNCTION
blocks.html:
• Heart efficiently pumps blood to meet metabolic demands
  • Normal preload and afterload
  • Adequate tissue perfusion
  • No fluid accumulation in lungs or periphery

blocks.heading: DYSFUNCTION
blocks.html:
• Heart unable to pump effectively (HFrEF) or fill properly (HFpEF)
  • Decreased cardiac output → SNS and RAAS activation
  • Vasoconstriction + sodium/water retention → fluid overload
  • Pulmonary congestion (left-sided) or systemic congestion (right-sided)

blocks.heading: ⚠ Risk Factors (Non-Modifiable)
blocks.html:
• Age >65
  • Family history cardiomyopathy
  • Previous MI (damaged myocardium)

blocks.heading: 💡 Risk Factors (Modifiable)
blocks.html:
• Hypertension (most common cause)
  • Coronary artery disease / prior MI
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Valvular heart disease
  • Chronic kidney disease
  • Obesity, sleep apnea, alcohol abuse

blocks.heading: 🔥 Complications
blocks.html: Acute pulmonary edema • Cardiogenic shock • Arrhythmias (AF, VT) • Hepatic congestion / cardiac cirrhosis • Renal failure (cardiorenal syndrome) • Cachexia (cardiac cachexia)
NRG Opposite: Heart cannot pump effectively → fluid backs up → pulmonary/systemic congestion → organ dysfunction

1. Initial insult: MI, HTN, valve disease damages myocardium

2. Decreased contractility (HFrEF) or compliance (HFpEF)

3. Reduced CO activates SNS: tachycardia + vasoconstriction

4. Reduced renal perfusion activates RAAS: Na+/H2O retention

5. ADH release: further fluid retention

6. Ventricular remodeling: dilation, hypertrophy, fibrosis

blocks.heading: Key Detail
blocks.html: HFrEF = reduced EF (<40%), dilated ventricle cannot contract forcefully. HFpEF = preserved EF (>50%), stiff ventricle cannot relax and fill properly. Both result in reduced forward flow and backward congestion.

blocks.heading: Clinical Result
blocks.html: Chronic compensation leads to ventricular remodeling (dilation, hypertrophy, fibrosis). Initially maintains CO but eventually decompensates. BNP rises as ventricles stretch. Forward failure = fatigue, weakness. Backward failure = pulmonary edema (left) or peripheral edema (right).
NRG Sequencing: Each step leads to the next — understand the cascade to predict S/S and management

blocks.heading: Early / Mild
blocks.html:
• Fatigue, weakness on exertion
  • Dyspnea on exertion (DOE)
  • Orthopnea (dyspnea when lying flat)
  • Nocturia
  • Mild peripheral edema (ankles)

blocks.heading: Severe
blocks.html:
• Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND)
  • Crackles throughout lung fields
  • Jugular venous distension
  • Hepatomegaly, ascites
  • S3 gallop (ventricular gallop)
  • Cyanosis, cool extremities

blocks.heading: Acute pulmonary edema: pink frothy sputum, severe dyspnea
blocks.html:
• Acute pulmonary edema: pink frothy sputum, severe dyspnea
  • Cardiogenic shock: BP <90, oliguria, altered LOC
  • Respiratory failure requiring intubation
  • THIS IS A MEDICAL EMERGENCY

blocks.heading: Diagnostic / Assessment Findings
blocks.html:
• BNP/NT-proBNP: elevated (>400 pg/mL diagnostic)
  • Chest X-ray: cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema, pleural effusions
  • Echocardiogram: reduced EF, wall motion abnormalities
  • ECG: may show LVH, prior MI changes
  • ABG: hypoxemia, respiratory alkalosis (compensatory hyperventilation)

blocks.heading: Link Patho to S/S
blocks.html:
Decreased CO → Fatigue, weakness, cool extremities

Pulmonary congestion → Dyspnea, crackles, orthopnea

RAAS activation → Edema, weight gain, JVD

Hepatic congestion → RUQ pain, elevated LFTs, ascites

blocks.heading: Cardiovascular
blocks.html:
• BP, HR, rhythm (listen for S3)
  • JVD assessment ( HF indicator)
  • Apical pulse, heart sounds
  • Peripheral edema (pitting scale 1-4+)
  • Daily weights (1 kg = 1 L fluid)
  • Hepatomegaly, ascites

blocks.heading: Respiratory
blocks.html:
• Respiratory rate, effort, SpO2
  • Lung sounds (crackles, wheezes)
  • Orthopnea — number of pillows
  • Cough (dry vs. productive pink frothy)

blocks.heading: Neurological
blocks.html:
• Mental status (cerebral perfusion)
  • Anxiety level
  • Sleep quality, PND episodes

blocks.heading: Key Laboratory & Diagnostic Tests
rows: Monitor K+ with diuretics — hypokalemia risk

blocks.heading: Priority Actions
blocks.html: Daily weights (same time, scale, clothing). Accurate I&O. Strict fluid restriction if ordered (typically 1.5-2 L/day). Sodium restriction (2g/day). Elevate HOB 30-45 degrees. Monitor for signs of fluid overload.

blocks.heading: Digoxin Toxicity Alert
blocks.html: Therapeutic range: 0.5-0.9 ng/mL. Toxicity risk increases with hypokalemia, renal impairment, elderly. Early signs: nausea, confusion, visual changes (yellow halos). Always check apical pulse x1 min before giving — hold if HR <60.

blocks.heading: Lifestyle & Patient Education
blocks.html:
• Daily weights — report gain >1-2 kg in 24h or >2-3 kg in 1 week
  • Sodium restriction <2g/day
  • Fluid restriction 1.5-2 L/day if severe
  • Medication adherence — NEVER stop diuretics abruptly
  • Recognize worsening symptoms early
🚨 Report Immediately: Weight gain >2 kg in 24h | Increasing dyspnea | New/worsening edema | S3 gallop | BNP rising | Decreased urine output

blocks.heading: Nursing Diagnosis
blocks.html: Decreased cardiac output related to impaired myocardial contractility as evidenced by fatigue, dyspnea, orthopnea, JVD, peripheral edema, and S3 gallop

blocks.heading: Goal / Outcome
blocks.html: Patient will demonstrate stable fluid balance (I&O within 500 mL, no weight gain >0.5 kg/day) and report decreased dyspnea within 48 hours.

blocks.heading: Interventions
blocks.html:
• Administer furosemide as prescribed — monitor response
  • Daily weights, strict I&O
  • Elevate HOB 30-45 degrees
  • Restrict sodium and fluids per orders
  • Monitor electrolytes (especially K+)
  • Assess lung sounds and edema q4h

blocks.heading: Rationale
blocks.html: Diuretics reduce fluid overload and pulmonary congestion. Daily weights detect fluid retention before clinical signs. HOB elevation reduces venous return to heart and improves breathing. Electrolyte monitoring prevents dangerous hypokalemia from diuretics.

blocks.heading: Evaluation
blocks.html: Weight decreased 1.5 kg. I&O negative 400 mL. Lung sounds clear bilaterally. No peripheral edema. Patient reports dyspnea 2/10 at rest. BNP trending down.
NRG Care Plan Formula: Problem → Goal → Interventions → Rationale → Evaluation

What system is being tested?

Cardiovascular — pump function and fluid status

What is the priority?

Fluid management — diuretics, daily weights, I&O, Na+/fluid restriction

What is unsafe?

Giving digoxin without checking pulse; stopping diuretics abruptly; missing daily weights

What restores function?

Reducing preload (diuretics) + afterload (ACE-I) + improving contractility (beta-blockers)

blocks.heading: 💡 Key Memory Aids for RENR
blocks.html:
• Left-sided HF: BACKS UP INTO LUNGS — think pulmonary edema, dyspnea, crackles
  • Right-sided HF: BACKS UP INTO BODY — think JVD, peripheral edema, hepatomegaly
  • Daily weights: 1 kg = 1 L fluid — most sensitive indicator of fluid status
  • Furosemide: Loop diuretic — monitor K+ (hypokalemia risk), I&O, hearing
  • BNP: >400 pg/mL = diagnostic of HF; tracks response to treatment
NRG System Focus Formula: Heart Failure → Cardiovascular → Pump dysfunction → Fluid overload → Priority: Reduce preload + afterload + monitor daily weights

question.stem: A patient with chronic heart failure is receiving furosemide 40 mg daily. The nurse notes the patient has gained 3 kg over 2 days, has bilateral crackles, and reports increasing shortness of breath. Which nursing intervention is the priority?

options.html: Increase the furosemide dose independently to promote diuresis
Notify the physician of the weight gain and worsening symptoms
Encourage the patient to drink more fluids to prevent dehydration
Restrict the patient's sodium intake and recheck weight in one week

question.rationale: A 3 kg weight gain over 2 days with bilateral crackles and worsening SOB indicates acute decompensated heart failure with fluid overload. The nurse must notify the physician promptly for medication adjustment (likely increased diuretic) and further evaluation. Independent dose changes are beyond nursing scope. Encouraging more fluids worsens overload. Delaying action for one week is unsafe.

why.html: Nurses cannot independently increase medication doses — requires physician order
More fluids worsen fluid overload and pulmonary edema
Delaying action for one week with acute decompensation is dangerous
